findings.title: Login IDP cache key omits organizationId, causing repeated invalidation/rebuild of one shared entry
findings.body: `cacheKeyForLogin(realm, mode)` only includes the realm id and the fetch mode, while the per-organization dimension is pushed into the `searchKey` of a single `IdentityProviderListQuery` entry. Consequently all organizations of a realm share one cache entry for `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`. Each time a login happens for an organization whose id is not yet in that entry, the code takes the `cached == null` branch and calls `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` and then re-adds a copy of the whole query object (lines 234-241). In a realm with many organizations this means (a) one cache entry that grows linearly with the number of organizations, (b) a full invalidate-and-rebuild of the shared entry on the first login of every new organization, and in a cluster nodes repeatedly discard each other's accumulated entry for different orgs. Contrast this with `getByOrganization`, where the organization id is part of the cache key, so each org gets its own entry. Including `organizationId` in the cache key (or keeping the entry append-only) would avoid the thrashing.

findings.title: Cleanup registers removal of a hard-coded alias "alias", so the 21 created IDPs are never deleted
findings.body: `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` (also at line 425) uses the literal string "alias" instead of the alias that was just created (`idp-alias-<i>` / `idp-alias-20`). The cleanup therefore targets a non-existent identity provider (producing a 404 on every cleanup callback) and none of the 21 identity providers created by `testCacheIDPForLogin` are removed. The leftover providers pollute the shared test realm, and since this test asserts exact counts of login-eligible providers (5, 10, 6, 11), leftovers from this or other tests in the same class (`testCacheIDPByOrg` has the same copy/paste defect at line 303) make the assertions dependent on JUnit method execution order and prone to intermittent failures.

findings.title: New invalidation paths on remove() and for non-public org brokers are untested
findings.body: The test only removes `idp-alias-1`, which is disabled and therefore not login-eligible, so the newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` call in `InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.remove()` is never exercised with a provider that actually appears in the login caches; a regression there (e.g. looking up the alias after deletion, or not invalidating at all) would leave a removed broker in the cached login list and would not be caught. Likewise, the new clause added to `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()` (organization-linked IDPs only count as login IDPs when `kc.org.broker.public` is true) is never covered: no test creates/removes an org-linked provider with `BROKER_PUBLIC=false` and asserts that the login caches are *not* invalidated.

findings.title: Update comparison mixes an organization-aware wrapper with a raw model, causing spurious cache invalidation
findings.body: `update()` obtains `original` via `getById(...)`, which (when the ORGANIZATION feature is enabled) returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass from `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel()` whose `isEnabled()` additionally reflects the state of the linked organization and of the OrganizationProvider. `updated` is the raw model coming from the caller, whose `isEnabled()` only reflects the IDP's own flag. So for any IDP linked to a *disabled* organization, `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` is false while `getLoginPredicate().test(updated)` is true, and `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate` will invalidate all three login cache entries on every unrelated update of that provider (e.g. a display-name change). This is only a performance/noise issue (over-invalidation), but it defeats the purpose of the fine-grained check; comparing the unwrapped model (or comparing only the persisted flags) would avoid it.
